newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Lindsey sees moderate growth, tame inflation.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Lindsey sees moderate growth, tame inflation.

text.p: Federal Reserve Governor Lawrence Lindsey on Sunday predicted that U.S. economic growth would remain moderate and that inflation would stay in check.

Asked by reporters about his outlook for the economy after an appearance at an American Economic Association conference here, Lindsey responded, "By and large, moderate growth is still the most likely scenario so far."
He was also asked if he expected inflation to remain tame, and replied, "All the evidence I see right now suggests that's the case."
Earlier, Fed Governor Laurence Meyer predicted trend growth of about two to 2-1/2 percent for 1997.
Asked if he agreed with that forecast, Lindsey declined to provide further details on his outlook, saying he was still formulating his forecast for this year.
However, Lindsey appeared content overall with the current state of the economy.
"It's hard to quarrel with 2-1/2 to three percent inflation (and) 5-1/4 percent unemployment," he said, adding, "It looks pretty good to me."
In a panel discussion at the conference, Lindsey was critical of the idea of adopting specific rules to govern monetary policy and the setting of interest rates.
"I think that people can do better than a rule," he said, adding that the process of determining monetary policy is much more complicated than can be encompassed in any specific rule.
Some economists recently proposed that the Fed adopt specific inflation targets to be used in determining interest rates, such as occurs in New Zealand.
Lindsey suggested that this approach would not be something he would favor. "Everything I said about rules applies even in that case," he said.
Lindsey's discussion of a rule-based monetary policy was part of broader remarks he made at the conference on the independence of the Fed.

He said there were two kinds of independence for a central bank -- independence from the political process and independence of economics, that is, the ability to operate without being constrained by a rule.

Lindsey said having "flesh and blood" individuals set policy by their own discretion had its advantages. They can be flexible, they can be blamed if there are problems, and they can fight back when the central bank is criticised.
Despite being independent, the Fed is still accountable to the public, Lindsey noted.

He said the Fed has gained a great deal of respect for the way it has conducted monetary policy over the past several years, heightening the institution's power and influence. But Lindsey said that could change.
"(The Fed is) above its long-run equilibrium with regard to power and influence ... That's probably not sustainable," the central banker said.
